editorial.headline: A Clear National Opening, but No PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers jamu houses and stalls serving herbal drinks, nationally open to full foreign ownership but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
A natural-medicine drink house or jamu stall is, at its core, a public-facing place to sell and serve herbal drinks or beverages made from natural medicinal ingredients. The activity may occupy part or all of a permanent building, whether or not it has equipment for making and storing the drinks. Its scope also reaches drink-service businesses preparing ready-to-consume jamu at a fixed site that can be moved or dismantled, commonly in a tented format. The practical point is the service of the drink to the public on the business premises: this is not merely a retail description, but an activity built around preparation and serving.

The registration field is broad on business scale. Micro, small, medium and large enterprises are all open to this activity. Nationally, it is classified as open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a full national opening: a foreign-owned company may hold the activity within the national PMA framework, subject only to the information stated for this code. For founders, the scale options matter because the activity can describe anything from a modest jamu counter to a larger operation, while the code’s national investment position remains fully open.

Bali changes the conclusion sharply. Today, a foreigner is unable to register this activity for PMA in Bali. At the large-business scale, the OSS risk classification is low or medium-low across every scope of the activity. Bali’s moratorium blocks all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities from PMA registration across the island, permanently; this code is therefore blocked under that rule. The record identifies the moratorium as taking effect in May 2026. The national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling is real, but it does not override Bali’s registration block for this activity.

That distinction deserves to be read plainly. National openness answers the ownership question for Indonesia at large; Bali’s moratorium answers whether the PMA registration can proceed on the island. Here, those answers point in different directions. The activity is nationally open across every listed scale, yet unavailable for PMA registration in Bali because its large-scale OSS risk treatment falls within the island-wide moratorium. For a founder considering a Bali-based jamu house or stall, the decisive current fact is not the national ownership ceiling but the Bali block.
editorial.pullQuote: The national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling is real, but it does not override Bali’s registration block for this activity.
